title: Royal Adelaide Hospital Study Abroad Report
paragraphs: At the Royal Adelaide Hospital in Australia I rotated through trauma and emergency, thoracic and cardiac surgery, and urology. During the clerkship I was able to observe the differences from Japan closely, and I had many opportunities to assist with procedures and to perform techniques myself, so it was fulfilling.

In the first month, trauma and emergency, the work was shift-based, so I was assigned to a different doctor every day. When a seriously injured patient was brought in, more than ten staff members in the Resuscitation Room briskly carried out their assigned tasks, and at first I was overwhelmed by the sight. At first it was also hard to follow the conversations, but gradually I could understand them, and when hands were short I sometimes felt that I had become a member of the team. There are many cases of traffic trauma, falls and drops, but people who have been stabbed with knives or shot with guns also sometimes come in, and I was also allowed to observe emergency surgery. Because Australia is a vast country with sparsely scattered residential areas, the medical catchment area that the Royal Adelaide Hospital supports is said to have a radius of about 3000 km. In fact, patients who had been in a traffic accident about 500 km away were sometimes brought in by helicopter ambulance, and I felt a major difference from Japan. The number of patients brought in varies from day to day, and severely ill patients may be brought in during the night, so from partway through I wanted to gain more experience and stayed on standby 24 hours a day.

In the second month, thoracic and cardiac surgery, students here generally seem to follow an intern and learn ward work, but I wanted to grasp the whole picture, so I was allowed to follow various doctors. Sometimes I watched them take consults from other departments and other hospitals, and sometimes I was allowed to observe procedures and surgery on the ward. On the ward I was given the opportunity to draw blood and place IV lines, and I tried to get as many opportunities as possible to interact with patients. The surgeries were mainly valve operations and coronary artery bypass operations, but they proceeded very quickly, and since I had the image that heart surgery takes a long time, I was greatly surprised by how short the operations were. A Japanese doctor was also working there and told me about the differences in cardiac surgery and patients between Japan and here, so it was very easy to do the clerkship. Once a week there is a joint round with the cardiology doctors, and there I was given the opportunity to present on "takotsubo cardiomyopathy." It was my first time and I was nervous, but I received good feedback from the doctors.

In the third month, urology, I mainly observed outpatient clinics and surgery. Here they handle urological diseases in general except for those in children, so I was able to learn broadly. The doctors were also kind and carefully taught me about diagnosis and treatment. I was also allowed to perform a flexible cystoscopy on an examination day, which was a good experience. In the third month I could also feel my English improving, and I enjoyed the clerkship. At the weekly conference, I learned a lot while listening to discussions on the imaging findings and treatment plans of difficult cases.

Over the three months I learned about the differences between Japan and Australia in the physician system, the insurance system and people's way of life. Here the length of hospital stay is very short, many surgeries are performed every day, and patients turn over quickly, so I had a hard time grasping all the patients in a short time, but it was a very good experience. It was also a good opportunity to think about what direction I want to take in the future.

Since I was the first exchange student to Australia, my study abroad started with almost no information, but I was able to meet Japanese doctors active in clinical work and research, and I think I spent fulfilling days while receiving their advice. In each department, too, I was blessed with truly kind doctors and staff, and I enjoyed the clerkship.
I am deeply grateful to the doctors of the International Exchange Office who gave me this wonderful opportunity and to everyone who supported my study abroad. Thank you very much.
